// how it works
UPGRADE 01 · REV A
Optical flow: The sensor sees floor texture move across its tiny image and reports pixel displacement per frame — the
angular rate of the ground beneath. It is a mouse sensor pointed at the floor from a metre up.
▸
Height turns flow into velocity: The same angular rate means a faster ground speed when you are higher, so the flight
controller needs the height from a rangefinder (a ToF like the VL53L1X or a TFmini) to scale flow into linear velocity.
▸
Fusion in the estimator: The flight controller’s EKF fuses flow velocity with the IMU and the rangefinder into a position
estimate whose drift is bounded by the flow — no GPS required. It also enables terrain-following altitude hold.
▸
Light and texture: Flow needs texture and light: a blank floor or a dim room starves it. A small downward LED and a
textured surface make the difference between a locked hover and a drift.
▸
Flight modes: With flow enabled, position-hold and loiter modes work indoors, and the controller arbitrates between GPS
and flow depending on what is healthy. Understanding that arbitration is what keeps a hybrid indoor / outdoor flight safe.
▸

PROJECT 1
Cold-Gas Reaction Thruster
A platform that rotates and holds its heading by firing puffs of compressed gas —
exactly like a spacecraft's RCS
Cost: ~$75
Difficulty: Advanced
Build Time: 2-3 weekends
Why This Matters
Out in orbit there is nothing to push against, so spacecraft change and hold their orientation by firing
small thrusters — the reaction control system (RCS). You can build the same thing on the ground:
mount a platform on a near-frictionless bearing, plumb a few small solenoid valves to a
compressed-gas supply, and fire short puffs to rotate it and hold a commanded heading. An IMU
senses the angle, a controller decides which thruster to pulse and for how long, and the platform slews
and stops on target — no wheels, no contact, just gas. This is exactly how satellites maneuver, and the
air-bearing version is literally how aerospace labs test real attitude-control hardware before flight. It is
the most viscerally 'spacecraft' project you can build on a bench.
What this proves to a recruiter: You understand reaction-control propulsion, closed-loop attitude
control, solenoid valve driving and pulse-width thrust modulation, and inertial sensing. Propulsion
and GNC are core spacecraft disciplines, and demonstrating thruster-based attitude control on an air
bearing is exactly the kind of hardware aerospace teams build and test.
→ The job this maps to: spacecraft propulsion and GNC — satellite and launch companies, and the
air-bearing test labs that validate attitude-control systems.
Safety: Compressed gas is genuinely dangerous. Use only a properly rated regulator and tubing,
never exceed component pressure ratings, and secure the gas supply so it cannot become a
projectile. Use inert gas (CO2 or filtered compressed air) — never anything flammable or an
unregulated high-pressure source — wear eye protection, and fully depressurize before working on
the plumbing.

===P2===
@1nska   •   6 EE Projects That Build a Real Satellite   •   Page 3
How It Works
• Newton's third law in a vacuum: A spacecraft cannot push against anything, so it carries its own
reaction mass: expel gas one way, the body rotates the other. Firing a thruster offset from the
center of mass produces a torque that slews the vehicle. Your bench version does the identical
thing on a low-friction bearing that mimics the freedom of orbit.
• Near-frictionless bearing: The platform sits on a ball bearing, a lazy-Susan, or — for the stretch
version — a planar air bearing that floats it on a thin film of air. The lower the friction, the more the
demo behaves like a real satellite, where the only torques are the ones you command.
• Solenoid 'thrusters': Small 12 V solenoid valves act as on/off thrusters. Mounted in opposing pairs
at the platform's edge and fed from a regulated gas line, each releases a puff of gas through a
nozzle when energized. Opposing pairs let you torque clockwise or counter-clockwise.
• Pulsed thrust control: You cannot throttle a solenoid, so you modulate thrust the way real RCS does
— by pulse width and pulse frequency. Short pulses give fine control near the target; longer or more
frequent pulses give a fast slew. The controller translates a commanded torque into a valve on-time.
• Closed-loop attitude control: An IMU measures the platform's angle and rate; a PD controller
computes the torque needed to reach and hold the setpoint, then thruster-selection logic fires the
correct valve. Because gas is limited, the controller must avoid a 'limit cycle' — chattering around
the target and wasting gas — which is a real spacecraft design problem.

PROJECT 1
ADS-B Aircraft Radar
Build a live map of every plane overhead — callsign, altitude, speed — pulled out of
the air onto your screen
Cost: ~$30
Difficulty:
Beginner-Intermediate
Build Time: 1 weekend
Why This Matters
Every airliner constantly broadcasts its identity, GPS position, altitude, and velocity in the clear on 1090
MHz — a system called ADS-B that is replacing radar for air-traffic control worldwide. There is no
encryption and no subscription: with a $30 software-defined radio and a small antenna, you can
receive those broadcasts directly and plot every aircraft in range on a live map, exactly like the
professional flight-tracking sites (which are largely built from volunteer receivers just like the one you
will build). It is the perfect first SDR project — the signal is strong, always present, and the payoff is
immediate and genuinely impressive: a real-time radar picture of the sky above you, decoded by
hardware you assembled.
What this proves to a recruiter: You understand SDR fundamentals, pulse-position-modulated
digital signals (Mode S), antenna selection for a specific band, and real-time packet decoding.
Receiving and decoding a live aviation datalink is a concrete, demonstrable RF skill that maps
straight onto avionics, surveillance, and wireless-systems work.
→ The job this maps to: air-traffic / surveillance systems, avionics, and SDR/RF engineering —
flight-tracking networks, air-navigation service providers, and aerospace firms.

===P2===
@1nska   •   6 EE Projects That Eavesdrop on the Sky   •   Page 3
How It Works
• ADS-B on 1090 MHz: Aircraft transponders broadcast 'extended squitter' messages roughly twice a
second containing the 24-bit ICAO address, GPS latitude/longitude, altitude, speed, and callsign.
The signals are unencrypted and standardised worldwide, so any compatible receiver can decode
them.
• Pulse-position modulation: Mode S encodes bits as the position of short pulses within each
microsecond — a 1 Mbit/s pulse-position-modulated stream. The decoder samples fast enough to
distinguish pulse timing, reconstruct the message bits, and check them with a CRC.
• Antenna tuned to 1090 MHz: At 1090 MHz a quarter-wave is only ~6.9 cm, so a small ground-plane
or 'spider' antenna works and a collinear gives more range. Antenna length and placement (high,
clear of obstructions) matter far more than fancy electronics on this band.
• LNA and filter help range: Distant aircraft are weak and the band sits near strong cellular and pager
interference. A 1090 MHz SAW filter plus a low-noise amplifier at the antenna dramatically extends
range — from tens to a couple hundred kilometres line-of-sight.
• Decode and map (dump1090): Software like dump1090 demodulates the Mode S stream, validates
each message by CRC, and converts the position fields into latitude/longitude. It serves a live
browser map showing every aircraft's callsign, altitude, heading, and trail — a real-time radar
display you built.

❯ project 01
H-Bridge DC Motor Driver
Spin a motor either direction at any speed you choose — the front end of every robot
$15
beginner
1 weekend
## why this matters
Before a robot can balance, drive, or steer, something has to turn a control signal into
torque. An H-bridge does exactly that: four switches that push current through a DC motor in
either direction, plus PWM that sets how hard. Build one, drive a motor forward and reverse,
ramp its speed smoothly, and sense the current it draws, and you have the power stage that
sits under every motor-control project in this guide. It is the cheapest, most fundamental
motor build, and the payoff is immediate — a motor that does exactly what your code says.
WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand H-bridge topology, PWM speed control, motor direction switching,
freewheeling and why inductive loads need it, and current sensing — the power-stage
foundation of motor-drive and robotics hardware.
→ the job this maps to: motor drives & robotics hardware — actuator, drone, and robotics
companies, and power-electronics teams.
## how it works
The H-bridge: Four switches arranged in an H around the motor. Close one diagonal pair and
current flows one way (forward); close the other pair and it reverses. Never close one
side’s top and bottom together — that is “shoot-through,” a dead short.
▸
PWM sets the speed: Rather than vary the voltage, you switch the bridge on and off
thousands of times a second. The duty cycle (fraction on) sets the average voltage and thus
the speed; the motor’s inductance smooths the pulses into steady torque.
▸
Freewheeling and flyback: A motor is inductive, so when you switch it off the current must
keep flowing somewhere. The bridge’s body diodes (or added flyback diodes) give it a path,
protecting the switches from voltage spikes — which is why an unprotected bridge dies fast.
▸
Driving it from logic: Two pins set direction and a PWM pin sets speed (or two PWM pins for
sign-magnitude drive). A driver IC (DRV8871, TB6612, L298) packages the bridge and gate
drive so you command it with logic levels.
▸
Sensing current: A small sense resistor (or the driver’s current output) tells you how hard
the motor is working. It is your window into torque, stalls, and faults — and the first
ingredient of closed-loop control.
▸

Flight controller from scratch
write your own attitude filter and PID loop on an ESP32 + MPU6050 and balance a one-axis
rig before you ever spin four props.
$18
intermediate

## why this matters
Every drone company assumes a graduate has only ever flashed Betaflight, and that assumption
is usually correct. This project forces you through the part the firmware hides: raw gyro
rates and accelerometer vectors coming in at 1 kHz, a complementary (or Kalman) filter turning
them into a roll and pitch angle, and a PID loop turning that angle error into motor commands.
You will discover that the textbook loop oscillates on a real rig, that the gyro drifts, that
the accelerometer lies under vibration, and that the difference between a stable hover and a
flip is a derivative term and a 100 Hz low-pass filter. Debugging that on a hinged one-axis
test stand, with a logged plot of setpoint versus measured angle, is the actual skill a
flight-controls engineer is hired for.
WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You can explain where your angle estimate comes from, why you fused gyro and
accelerometer instead of trusting either, what your loop rate is and why, and what the
D-term does when the motor response is slow. You tuned gains on real hardware with a
logged step response, not a slider in a simulator. That is a control-systems story a
drone company can check in one question — and almost no one walks in with it.
→ the job this maps to: Flight controls / GNC engineer — attitude estimation and inner-loop
stabilization for multirotors.
SAFETY WARNING
Run every test with propellers removed until the rig is stable on the stand; a loop that
saturates will spin motors to full throttle without warning.
## how it works
▸ Two sensors, two failure modes: the gyro gives clean rate but integrates into drift; the
accelerometer gives an absolute tilt but is swamped by motor vibration — the filter trusts
the gyro fast and the accelerometer slow.
▸ Loop rate sets the ceiling: a 250 Hz loop can stabilize a rig whose dynamics are 10–20 Hz;
go slower and the phase lag alone will make a well-tuned loop oscillate.
▸ Derivative on measurement, not error: putting D on the error makes every setpoint step a
spike to the motors; on the measurement it only reacts to what the rig is actually doing.
▸ Motor response is part of the plant: a brushless motor plus ESC has 30–80 ms of lag, which
is why the same gains that work in simulation oscillate on the bench.
▸ A test stand is not a cheat: every real flight-controller team tunes inner loops on a
constrained rig first — crashing a rig costs nothing, crashing an airframe costs a week.

PROJECT 1
GOES Earth Receiver
Pull a live, full-disk image of the entire planet off a satellite parked 36,000 km up
Cost: ~$75
Difficulty: Advanced
Build Time: 2-3 weekends
Why This Matters
GOES (Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites) are the spacecraft behind every weather
forecast you have ever seen. They sit in geostationary orbit 35,786 km above the equator, locked to
one spot on Earth, and continuously broadcast imagery back down on an L-band downlink near 1.69
GHz. The operational satellites — GOES-19 (East) and GOES-18 (West) — transmit a signal called
HRIT that anyone can receive with a software-defined radio, a low-noise amplifier, and a dish you can
build from hardware-store parts. Because the satellite never moves relative to the ground, you aim your
antenna once and leave it — no tracking motor. The challenge is pure RF: the signal arrives near the
thermal noise floor after a 36,000 km trip, so the whole link budget hinges on a clean, low-noise front
end and enough antenna gain to close the link.
What this proves to a recruiter: You understand L-band RF, low-noise amplifier and noise-figure
design, link budgets, antenna gain, and digital demodulation of a BPSK downlink. These are the
exact skills behind satellite communications, GPS, radar, and every space-to-ground link in the
industry.

===P2===
@1nska   •   6 EE Projects That Reach Space   •   Page 3
How It Works
• Geostationary downlink (1.69 GHz): GOES-East (GOES-19) and GOES-West (GOES-18)
broadcast HRIT near 1694.1 MHz. The signal is BPSK at roughly 400 kSym/s and carries full-disk
Earth images, regional mesoscale scans, and weather products.
• Antenna — gain is everything: After a 36,000 km path the signal is extremely weak, so you need
directional gain. A repurposed 2.4 GHz WiFi grid dish, a small offset satellite dish with a helical
feed, or a DIY cookware reflector all work. Because the bird is geostationary, you point once and
bolt it down.
• Low-noise amplifier + SAW filter: An LNA with a sub-1 dB noise figure, mounted right at the
antenna feed, sets the system sensitivity. A SAW filter near 1.69 GHz rejects cellular and WiFi that
would otherwise desensitize the receiver. This LNA-at-the-antenna placement is the single most
important decision in the build.
• Bias tee + SDR: A bias tee injects DC up the coax to power the LNA at the mast while passing RF
down to the radio. An RTL-SDR (or Airspy for more headroom) digitizes the filtered signal and
streams IQ samples to a laptop or Raspberry Pi.
• Demodulation + decode (SatDump): SatDump locks the BPSK carrier, recovers symbol timing,
applies Viterbi and Reed-Solomon forward error correction, and reassembles the packets into
full-disk and mesoscale images — the same pictures meteorologists use, pulled out of the air by
you.
Key Design Decisions
→ Why an LNA at the antenna instead of at the radio? Coax loss at 1.7 GHz is severe — several
dB per meter of cheap cable. Every dB of loss before the first amplifier adds directly to your noise
figure, so you amplify before the lossy cable degrades the signal.
→ Why geostationary instead of polar? A geostationary satellite appears fixed in the sky, so a
high-gain, narrow-beam dish can be aimed once and left. A polar satellite races across the sky and
would demand a motorized tracker — which is exactly Project 3's problem.
→ Why BPSK for the downlink? BPSK is the most power-efficient digital modulation — it tolerates
the lowest signal-to-noise ratio of any common scheme. When you are link-budget starved from
36,000 km, you trade data rate for the robustness that lets the link close at all.

Doppler Motion Radar
Wave your hand and watch its speed appear — the Doppler core inside every radar
$20
beginner

## why this matters
Every radar on Earth starts with one idea: a moving object shifts the frequency of the radio
it reflects. A pocket microwave module like the HB100 transmits a steady ~10.5 GHz tone and
mixes it with the echo, and what comes out is an audio-frequency “beat” whose pitch is
directly proportional to the target’s speed. Amplify that beat, sample it on an Arduino, run
an FFT, and you can read how fast your hand — or a passing person — is moving, in real time.
It is the cheapest possible way to build genuine radar, the payoff is immediate and visual,
and it is the foundation every later project in this guide builds on.
WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand the Doppler effect, continuous-wave radar, mixing down to baseband, low-
noise audio amplification, and basic FFT-based spectral estimation on a microcontroller
— the literal core of radar signal processing.
→ the job this maps to: radar & sensing engineering — automotive, security / occupancy
sensing, and defense radar groups.
## how it works
Continuous-wave Doppler: The HB100 transmits an unmodulated ~10.525 GHz carrier and mixes
the returning echo with it. A stationary target returns the same frequency (zero beat); a
moving target returns a Doppler-shifted frequency, and the mixer outputs the difference — a
low audio tone.
▸
The Doppler equation: The beat frequency is fd = 2·v·f₀/c. At 10.5 GHz, every 1 m/s of
radial speed produces ~70 Hz of beat, so walking speed (~1.5 m/s) lands near 100 Hz —
squarely in the audio band, which is why a cheap op-amp can handle it.
▸
Amplifying microvolts: The raw IF output is tiny (microvolts to millivolts) and low-
frequency. A two-stage op-amp with band-pass shaping (roughly 20 Hz–3 kHz) lifts it to a
clean line level the ADC can read, while rejecting DC offset and mains hum.
▸
Sampling and the FFT: An Arduino or ESP32 samples the amplified beat at a few kHz and runs
an FFT. The peak bin is the dominant Doppler frequency; convert it back to m/s with the
equation and you have a live speed readout.
▸
Reading direction (bonus): A plain HB100 cannot tell approaching from receding (both shift
the magnitude up). Modules with I/Q outputs, or an added quadrature mixer, recover the sign
of the shift — the same trick higher-end Doppler sensors use.
▸

## how it works
▸
Trilateration from time: Each satellite broadcasts its position and an extremely precise time. The receiver measures how long each signal took to
arrive, converts that to a distance, and solves for its own position where the ranges intersect — needing at least four satellites to also solve for its
own clock error.
▸
Time is the real product: Because position comes from timing, GNSS is first a time system. The satellites carry atomic clocks and the receiver
recovers time to nanoseconds — which is why GNSS quietly synchronises power grids, cell networks, and financial systems, and why time itself is a
defense priority.
▸
Below the noise floor: The signal arriving at your antenna is weaker than the background noise. The receiver recovers it by correlating against each
satellite's known pseudo-random code (a spread-spectrum trick) — a huge processing gain that pulls the signal up out of the noise.
▸
Reading the output: A receiver module outputs standard NMEA sentences over serial: position, altitude, speed, satellites in view, and fix quality.
Parsing these is your window into what the receiver is actually doing.
▸
Why it is fragile: The received power is tiny, so a small interferer can jam it, and because the format is public, a fake stronger signal can spoof it. Real
systems defend with directional and adaptive antennas, multi-constellation receivers, and spoofing detection — the resilience side of PNT.

// how it works
SP01 · 22.4 °C · ε 0.95
Fields stop at a conductor: A conductive shell redistributes charge and induces currents that cancel an external field
inside. At radio frequencies a thin conductive layer is enough — the field only penetrates to the “skin depth,” microns at
GHz.
▸
Apertures leak: Shielding fails at holes and seams, not through the metal. Any gap longer than a fraction of the
wavelength acts as a slot antenna and lets the field in — which is why gaskets, overlapping seams, and fine mesh matter
more than thick walls.
▸
Measuring attenuation: Put a known signal outside (WiFi, a broadcast station, a small legal ISM transmitter) and measure
inside with an SDR. The drop, in dB, is your shielding effectiveness — and every 20 dB is a tenfold reduction in field
strength.
▸
EMP and lightning: A nuclear EMP or a nearby lightning strike is a fast, enormous field pulse. Hardened systems combine
a shielded enclosure with filtered entry points and surge protection, because the shield is only as good as its weakest
cable.
▸
Shield, filter, ground: A complete hardening strategy layers three things: shield the enclosure, filter every wire that
crosses it, and manage the grounding so currents flow around the electronics rather than through them.

You understand optical flow (velocity from image motion), why flow must be scaled by height, how a flight controller’s
estimator fuses a new sensor, and how to configure and validate that fusion safely. That is the core of GPS-denied

// how it works
UPGRADE 01 · REV A
Optical flow: The sensor sees floor texture move across its tiny image and reports pixel displacement per frame — the
angular rate of the ground beneath. It is a mouse sensor pointed at the floor from a metre up.
▸
Height turns flow into velocity: The same angular rate means a faster ground speed when you are higher, so the flight
controller needs the height from a rangefinder (a ToF like the VL53L1X or a TFmini) to scale flow into linear velocity.
▸
Fusion in the estimator: The flight controller’s EKF fuses flow velocity with the IMU and the rangefinder into a position
estimate whose drift is bounded by the flow — no GPS required. It also enables terrain-following altitude hold.
▸
Light and texture: Flow needs texture and light: a blank floor or a dim room starves it. A small downward LED and a
textured surface make the difference between a locked hover and a drift.
▸
Flight modes: With flow enabled, position-hold and loiter modes work indoors, and the controller arbitrates between GPS
and flow depending on what is healthy. Understanding that arbitration is what keeps a hybrid indoor / outdoor flight safe.

PROJECT 1
AI Voice Cloning Detector
Analog circuit that detects AI-generated voices — no software, no ML model
Cost: ~$15
Difficulty:
Intermediate-Advanced
Build Time: 1-2 weekends
Why This Matters
AI voice cloning has reached the point where human ears can't tell the difference. But cloned audio has
measurable artifacts: spectral energy gaps in the 2-4kHz range, unnatural phase continuity, and
missing micro-variations that exist in real vocal cords. This project detects those artifacts using pure
analog signal processing — no machine learning model, no microcontroller.
The key insight: Real voices have chaotic, broadband energy with natural spectral
variation. AI clones have suspiciously smooth spectral envelopes because the
synthesis model interpolates between training samples. An analog filter bank can
measure this difference in real time.
System Architecture
How It Works

===P2===
@1nska  •  6 AI-Era EE Projects  •  Page 3
• Microphone + pre-amp: Electret mic with JFET buffer, then an AGC stage (LM386 or OPA344)
to normalize input levels regardless of speaker volume.
• Bandpass filter bank (8 bands): Eight parallel 2nd-order Sallen-Key bandpass filters covering
200Hz to 8kHz. Each band is ~1 octave wide. Center frequencies: 250, 500, 1K, 1.5K, 2K, 3K,
4.5K, 7KHz.
• Peak detectors: Each filter output feeds a diode peak detector with ~50ms decay time. This
gives a DC voltage proportional to energy in each band.
• Comparator array: Compares adjacent band energies and checks for suspicious gaps. Real
voices: smooth roll-off, adjacent bands within 6dB. AI clones: sharp dips between bands,
especially 2-4kHz.
• Decision logic: If more than 2 adjacent-band ratios exceed threshold, a simple logic gate
(74HC08 AND) triggers the RED LED. Otherwise, GREEN stays lit.
Key Design Decisions
→ Why 8 bands, not 16? More bands = more components but diminishing returns. 8
octave-spaced bands capture the spectral envelope accurately enough to detect synthesis artifacts
while keeping the circuit on a single PCB.
→ Why Sallen-Key topology? Unity-gain Sallen-Key filters use only 2 resistors and 2 caps per
stage. Low component count, good stability, and the op-amp doesn't need to provide gain (reduces
noise).
→ Why analog, not digital? An MCU with FFT could do this, but the point is demonstrating that
signal processing IS circuit design. In an interview, explaining why you chose each filter's Q factor
and center frequency is far more impressive than 'I used an FFT library.'

PROJECT 1
Laser Surveillance Microphone
Hear through a window from 100m — no mic in the room, no RF, no trace
Cost: ~$15
Difficulty: Advanced
Build Time: 1-2 weekends
Why This Matters
During the Cold War, intelligence agencies developed laser listening devices that could extract audio
from vibrating surfaces at distance. The principle is simple: sound waves inside a room cause the
window glass to vibrate by nanometers. An IR laser bouncing off that window is phase-modulated by
the vibration. A sensitive photodetector reads that modulation, and an FM demodulator extracts the
audio. The technique was declassified decades ago, but the analog design challenges remain:
sub-millivolt signal detection, laser intensity stabilization, and FM demodulation of an extremely weak
carrier.
What this proves to a recruiter: You understand optical signal chains, laser driver
design, transimpedance amplification at the noise floor, and analog FM
demodulation. These skills directly apply to LIDAR, fiber optics, optical sensing, and
defense.
System Architecture

===P2===
@1nska  •  Defense Tech Part 2: Laser + Covert Systems  •  Page 3
How It Works
• IR laser diode (808nm): A collimated infrared laser aimed at a window pane. The laser must be
intensity-stabilized using an APC (automatic power control) circuit — a monitor photodiode inside
the laser package feeds back to the driver, keeping output power constant. Any intensity drift
appears as noise in the received signal.
• Window vibration: Sound waves inside the room cause the glass to vibrate. A normal
conversation at 60dB SPL causes ~1-10nm of displacement on a window pane. This displacement
phase-modulates the reflected laser beam — the path length changes by twice the displacement
(there and back), creating a Doppler shift proportional to the velocity of the glass surface.
• Photodetector + TIA: A large-area silicon photodiode (BPW34 or similar) with a transimpedance
amplifier (1MΩ feedback) captures the reflected beam. The DC component represents the average
reflected power. The AC component (microvolts) carries the audio information. A coupling
capacitor separates them.
• Bandpass filter (300Hz-3kHz): A 4th-order Sallen-Key bandpass isolates the speech band. This
removes laser noise below 300Hz and high-frequency detector noise above 3kHz.
• FM demodulator: The phase modulation from the window vibration is equivalent to FM. A simple
PLL-based FM demodulator (LM567 or NE567) or a slope detector (tuned LC circuit on the slope
of the resonance curve) extracts the audio. Amplify and output to speaker or ADC.
Key Design Decisions
→ Why 808nm instead of visible laser? 808nm is invisible to the human eye — the target
doesn't know they're being illuminated. It also avoids eye safety concerns at low power levels and
matches common, cheap laser diodes.
→ Why APC on the laser driver? Without intensity stabilization, laser power fluctuations appear
as amplitude noise that masks the tiny phase modulation signal. The APC loop must have
bandwidth >10kHz to track fast intensity variations.
→ Why FM demodulation, not AM? The window vibration modulates the phase/frequency of the
reflected beam, not the amplitude. Amplitude changes come from beam wander and atmospheric
scintillation — these are noise sources, not signal. FM demodulation rejects AM noise inherently.

## the six steps
STEP 01
Skip the theory at first. Get a breadboard and an Arduino kit.
DO THIS
Buy a starter kit, not individual parts. A $30–40 Arduino Uno clone kit gives you the
board, a breadboard, jumper wires, a resistor assortment, LEDs, buttons, a buzzer, a
potentiometer and a few sensors — everything for the first month.
THE TRAP
Buying a 'proper' bench setup before you know what you'll use. A $200 oscilloscope on
day one teaches you nothing; a $2 LED does.
YOU'RE DONE WHEN
The kit is on your desk and the Arduino IDE (or PlatformIO) is installed and sees the
board.
STEP 02
Blink an LED. Then a buzzer. Then a button.
DO THIS
Upload the Blink example, then change the delay from 1000 ms to 100 ms and watch it
change. Wire an LED with a 220 ohm resistor on pin 13. Add the buzzer with tone().
Add a button with pinMode(INPUT_PULLUP) so the LED only lights while it's pressed.
THE TRAP
Copy-pasting a whole project on day two. Every build here is under 15 lines — type
them, break them, fix them.
YOU'RE DONE WHEN
You can make the LED, the buzzer and the button work together without looking
anything up.
STEP 03
Now learn the theory you just used.
DO THIS
You've already used Ohm's law (that 220 ohm resistor), Kirchhoff's laws (the current
through your LED loop) and a pull-up resistor. Go back and read exactly those: V =
IR, series vs parallel, voltage dividers, why the LED needs a resistor at all. The
concepts stick because you've held the parts.
THE TRAP
Trying to finish a 900-page textbook before touching a wire. Read one chapter, build
one thing, repeat.
YOU'RE DONE WHEN
You can calculate the resistor for any LED from its datasheet and explain why 5 V
straight into an LED kills it.

===P2===
the build list · @1nska
3
STEP 04
Learn to solder early. It's easier than it looks.
DO THIS
A $20 temperature-controlled iron, 0.8 mm leaded or lead-free solder, flux and a
practice kit (a $5 through-hole 'skill kit'). Tin the tip, heat the pad and the leg
together for two seconds, feed solder into the joint, not the iron. Twenty joints and
you'll have it.
THE TRAP
Waiting until a project 'needs' soldering. Breadboards fall apart the moment you move
them — soldering is what makes something yours to keep.
YOU'RE DONE WHEN
Your joints look like small shiny cones, not grey blobs, and a soldered LED circuit
works first try.
STEP 05
Measure everything. Multimeter first, oscilloscope later.
DO THIS
A $15 multimeter answers 90% of beginner questions: is there voltage here, is this
wire actually connected (continuity beep), how much current does this draw. Measure
your LED circuit and compare with what Ohm's law predicted. Only reach for a scope
when you start caring about signals over time (PWM, serial, audio).
THE TRAP
Guessing. 'It doesn't work' is not a diagnosis. 'Pin 13 is at 4.9 V but the LED anode
is at 0 V' is — and that takes ten seconds with a meter.
YOU'RE DONE WHEN
You debug by measuring before you debug by re-wiring.
STEP 06
Build one real project you actually want to use.
DO THIS
Not a tutorial — something with a job: a plant-moisture alarm, a desk lamp that dims
with a knob, a door sensor that texts you, a temperature logger for your room. Pick
one, make a parts list, build it on a breadboard, then solder it onto perfboard and
put it in a box.
THE TRAP
Ten half-finished projects. One finished thing you use every day teaches more than
ten demos, and it's the one you'll show people.
YOU'RE DONE WHEN
It's been running on your desk for a week and you've fixed at least one thing that
broke.
